title: The Minister Who Spoke Only in Proverbs (ML)
summary: An obnoxious courtier answers every state crisis by quoting ancient proverbs without taking action. Birbal cures him with an empty proverb feast. [ML]
full_text:
A pedantic courtier named Mirza Luqman was infamous across Agra for answering every single question, crisis, and petition by reciting well-known proverbs, never offering practical assistance.

When a peasant's crops flooded, Luqman remarked: 'Every cloud has a silver lining!'

When a merchant was robbed, Luqman sighed: 'Easy come, easy go!'

When the royal granaries caught fire, Luqman announced: 'Where there is smoke, there is fire!'

Emperor Akbar was thoroughly irritated by the minister's useless platitudes: 'Birbal, this man fills the air with wise sayings, yet does not lift a single finger to solve a problem! How can we cure him?'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, let us treat him with his own medicine.'

That afternoon, Birbal invited Mirza Luqman to a private banquet in the palace gardens. Luqman arrived, hungry and expectant.

Birbal placed an empty porcelain bowl before the minister and said: 'Dig in, noble Mirza!'

Luqman blinked: 'My lord, the bowl is empty! Where is the food?'

Birbal smiled pleasantly: 'Ah, Mirza Sahib! As the ancient sages say: "A contented mind is a perpetual feast!" Eat your contentment!'

Luqman's stomach rumbled: 'Yes, but I am physically hungry! I need real bread!'

Birbal nodded solemnly: 'True, but remember: "Man does not live by bread alone!"'

Luqman began to plead: 'Please, Birbal, just a cup of lentil soup!'

Birbal quoted: '"Too many cooks spoil the broth!"'

'Just a sip of cool water, then!'

Birbal replied: '"Still waters run deep!"'

Mirza Luqman sat clutching his starving belly, completely humiliated and exasperated, while Emperor Akbar watched from the balcony, laughing until tears ran down his face!

Luqman threw up his hands: 'I surrender, Raja Birbal! I understand your point! Proverbs are lovely ornaments for speech, but they cannot bake bread, put out fires, or govern an empire!'

Birbal then ordered a lavish feast served to the humbled courtier, who learned to offer practical action instead of hollow cliches.
